name: Kilishi
summary: Paper-thin sun-dried or oven-dried beef coated in a fiery peanut and spice paste, then grilled until chewy.
story: Kilishi is a Hausa dried-meat snack from northern Nigeria, often described as a spicier cousin of jerky. It is sold in markets and given as a gift, and is eaten on its own as a snack.

items.name: lean beef (topside or silverside)
items.note: in one or two thick pieces

steps.title: Freeze the meat
steps.text: Trim all fat and sinew. Wrap the beef and freeze for about 1.5 hours until firm but not solid; this makes slicing paper-thin possible.

steps.title: Slice thinly
steps.text: Cut the meat against or with the grain into slices about 2-3 mm thick. A very sharp knife helps. The slices should be thin enough to see light through.

steps.title: First drying
steps.text: Lay the slices on racks in a single layer. Dry in a 70 C (160 F) oven with the door slightly ajar for 1.5-2 hours, turning once, until the meat is dry, leathery and no longer wet.

steps.title: Mix the yaji
steps.text: Combine all paste ingredients in a bowl, adding water a spoonful at a time, until it is a thick, spreadable paste like soft peanut butter. Taste a tiny bit and adjust salt.

steps.title: Coat the meat
steps.text: Spread the paste thinly on both sides of each slice. Do not leave thick lumps because they cook unevenly.

steps.title: Second drying
steps.text: Return the coated slices to the oven at 70 C for 1 hour, turning once, until the surface feels dry and tacky.

steps.title: Grill to finish
steps.text: Brush lightly with oil and grill or broil briefly for 1-2 minutes per side until fragrant and lightly charred at the edges. Watch closely as thin meat burns fast.

steps.title: Cool and store
steps.text: Cool completely on a rack, then store in an airtight container. It should be firm and chewy, not brittle or soft.

tips: Fat spoils dried meat, so trim thoroughly.
Uniform thin slices are what make or break kilishi.
Dry thoroughly before storing to prevent mould; it keeps about 2-3 weeks in a cool place.
Scale heat with the cayenne; traditional kilishi is quite hot.

swaps.swap: Peanut butter (no sugar) thinned with a little oil works; allergy sufferers can use toasted sesame paste but the taste differs.
Traditionally sun-dried; a low oven or dehydrator is the practical alternative outside hot climates.
